messages.author: 9d7e54e3329f305f
messages.subject: assigning random effects to observations
parts:
Hello again all,

I'm playing around with a model that has a random effect for each US state, with seven observations over time for each state. So, there's a vector of 51 random effects in a GMRF/CAR structure (based off of the GeoBUGS lip cancer model I've discussed on the list previously), and they in turn need to be factored into the likelihoods of 357 datapoints. 

I've tried a few different methods and am curious as to what you'd recommend as the best method for Stan.

The first thing I tried was just looping through each observation to add in its random effects, as one would do in BUGS (attached as CAR_model_loop.stan.txt):

for (n in 1:N) {
    s <- state[n];
    beta1_long[n] <- beta1_stz[s];
}

this works, but I thought I should try to vectorize if possible and remove the loop.

So next (in CAR_model_matrix.stan.txt) I built a binary matrix[357,51] that when multiplied by beta_stz[51] gives the filled in random effects for each observation:

matrix[N,S] state_mat;
for (n in 1:N)
    for (s in 1:S)
        state_mat[n,s] <- if_else(state[n]==s, 1.0, 0.0);

beta1_long <- state_mat * beta1_stz;

I was surprised to find this takes about 3x longer than the looping version.

In PyMC I've always found a slight speedup using the matrix version. And by switching to sparse matrix libraries for state_mat in python I get an order of magnitude further speedup or more.

Any suggestions on how to best handle these types of operations in Stan? Thanks again!

>
> I've tried a few different methods and am curious as to what you'd recommend as the best method for Stan.
>
> The first thing I tried was just looping through each observation to add in its random effects, as one would do in BUGS
> (attached as CAR_model_loop.stan.txt):
>
> |
> for (n in 1:N) {
> s <- state[n];
> beta1_long[n] <- beta1_stz[s];
> }
> |
>
> this works, but I thought I should try to vectorize if possible and remove the loop.
>
> So next (in CAR_model_matrix.stan.txt) I built a binary matrix[357,51] that when multiplied by beta_stz[51] gives the
> filled in random effects for each observation:
>
> |
> matrix[N,S] state_mat;
> for (n in 1:N)
> for (s in 1:S)
> state_mat[n,s] <- if_else(state[n]==s, 1.0, 0.0);
> |
>
> |
> beta1_long <- state_mat * beta1_stz;
> |
>
> I was surprised to find this takes about 3x longer than the looping version.

Loops are very very fast in Stan -- they just get compiled to
C++ and most modern CPUs can easily parallelize the integer arithmetic
and comparisons in the loop and any floating point/assignments within
the loop.

The matrix operations are relatively slow because it's doing a ton of
extra work because of the sparsity.

We are going to add sparse matrix data types eventually, at which point
the matrix version might be faster.

The real issue is whether the operations are working exclusively
on variables declared in data or transformed data, or whether
they involve parameters (parameter, transformed parameter, local
variable in transformed parameter, or local variable in model block).

With parameters, so-called "reduction" operations that have a single
output are much faster when vectorized because we can vectorize the gradient calc,
which is otherwise slow.

So if either x or y is a parameter or transformed parameter of a local
variable declared in the model or transformed parameter

vector[N] x;
vector[N] y;
real sum;
...
sum <- 0;
for (n in 1:N)

sum <- sum + x[n] * y[n];

is much slower than

sum <- x' * y;

which is in turn a little bit slower than

sum <- dot_product(x,y);


On the other hand, you won't see much difference
between:

z <- exp(x);

and
for (n in 1:N)

z[n] <- exp(x[n]);

because we can't vectorize the gradients because of the
multiple outputs for z[n], which need to be stored and
reasoned about independently.

> In PyMC I've always found a slight speedup using the matrix version. And by switching to sparse matrix libraries for
> state_mat in python I get an order of magnitude further speedup or more.

That's because loops are slow in Python (unless you're using
something like Cython that compiles them to C++).
> Any suggestions on how to best handle these types of operations in Stan? Thanks again!

I hope that helps. If not, please keep asking questions!

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] assigning random effects to observations
parts:
It's not just C++ and it's not just loops. Modern
compilers try to execute a pipeline of instructions in
parallel. The biggest performance costs are for branches
that can't be predicted and expensive operations like
math lib calls or even division.

A good compiler can help lay out instructions to make
the CPU's job easier.

If you want to know more, Agner Fog's free online book on
optimizing C++ is great and it discusses both hardware and C++
in particular:

http://www.agner.org/optimize/optimizing_cpp.pdf

Just don't take the comments about the evils of templates too
seriously.

We've tried to be fairly careful in laying out Stan, but
there's a lot of room for improvement, and we're getting
some expert help in that direction.

- Bob

If you want to know more, Agner Fog's free online book on
optimizing C++ is great and it discusses both hardware and C++
in particular:

Thanks, Bob, adding that to the reading list! 

On a somewhat related note, when I'm generating interim quantities in a model like this, is there a way to store the final quantity but not the intermediate ones?

For instance, I'd like to store the traces of log_mu
log_mu <- log_pop + alpha0 + (alpha1 * year) + beta1_long;

but I don't need beta1_long or beta1_stz
beta1_stz <- beta1 - mean(beta1);
for (n in 1:N) {

beta1_long[n] <- beta1_stz[state[n]];

In order to move log_mu from model to transformed parameters, I have to also put beta1_stz and beta1_long there. (Otherwise they're of course out of scope and log_mu can't be computed in transformed parameters).

If I instead try to generate a new quantity from log_mu in generated quantities I get an error that log_mu doesn't exist, since it's local to the model block.
generated quantities {
    vector[N] mu;
    mu <- exp(log_mu);
}

The only way I can think to save log_mu without also storing beta1_stz/beta1_long is to bypass them altogether, but that prevents vectorization:
transformed parameters {
    vector[N] log_mu;
for (n in 1:N)

log_mu[n] <- log_pop[n] + alpha0 + (alpha1 * year[n]) + (beta1[state[n]] - mean(beta1));
}

Based on the manual and this thread I'm guessing my only option is to also store the interim quantities by putting them all in the transformed parameters block. Is that accurate? Not a big deal for this model, just keeping an eye towards my eventual model which is huge...

On 4/4/13 8:09 PM, Kyle Foreman wrote:
> If you want to know more, Agner Fog's free online book on
> optimizing C++ is great and it discusses both hardware and C++
> in particular:
>
>
> Thanks, Bob, adding that to the reading list!
>
> On a somewhat related note, when I'm generating interim quantities in a model like this, is there a way to store the
> final quantity but not the intermediate ones?

The only values saved during sampling are variables
declared in the parameters block, in the transformed parameters
block, or in the generated quantities block.

So define what you want to save in one of those blocks,
and define everything else as a local variable.

>
> For instance, I'd like to store the traces of log_mu
> |
> log_mu <- log_pop + alpha0 + (alpha1 * year) + beta1_long;
> |
>
> but I don't need beta1_long or beta1_stz
> |
> beta1_stz <- beta1 - mean(beta1);
> for (n in 1:N) {
> beta1_long[n] <- beta1_stz[state[n]];
> |

That's fine. Declare beta1_long and beta1_stz as local variables
and they won't be written out. They can still be used to define
log_mu, and log_mu will still be visible outside the transformed
parameter block.

> In order to move log_mu from model to transformed parameters, I have to also put beta1_stz and beta1_long there.
> (Otherwise they're of course out of scope and log_mu can't be computed in transformed parameters).

Right. Which means they won't be visible in the model
block.

> If I instead try to generate a new quantity from log_mu in generated quantities I get an error that log_mu doesn't
> exist, since it's local to the model block.
> |
> generated quantities {
> vector[N] mu;
> mu <- exp(log_mu);
> }
> |
>
> The only way I can think to save log_mu without also storing beta1_stz/beta1_long is to bypass them altogether, but that
> prevents vectorization:
> |
> transformed parameters {
> vector[N] log_mu;
> for (n in 1:N)
> log_mu[n] <- log_pop[n] + alpha0 + (alpha1 * year[n]) + (beta1[state[n]] - mean(beta1));
> }
> |

I'm not sure what you mean by "prevents vectorization". What
gets saved is orthogonal to what's vectorized.

> Based on the manual and this thread <https://groups.google.com/d/msg/stan-users/lybDQTpMWRw/QduePUFLcp0J> I'm guessing

> my only option is to also store the interim quantities by putting them all in the transformed parameters block. Is that
> accurate? Not a big deal for this model, just keeping an eye towards my eventual model which is huge...

Can you send a working model that perhaps saves too much
and indicate which variables you want to save? It's hard
to tell from code fragments.

You can (re)define whatever you want in generated quantities and
it'll get saved. The generated quantities are only computed
once per iteration, not once per leapfrog step, and they're
computed with double values rather than auto-dif variables for
gradients, so they're much faster. The problem is that it
can require redundant definitions.

For example, you can add this to generated quantities and log_mu
will get saved:

generated quantities {

vector[N] log_mu;
for (n in 1:N)
log_mu[n] <- log_pop[n] + alpha0 + (alpha1 * year[n]) + (beta1[state[n]] - mean(beta1));

That is, assuming everything on the right side is either data, a parameter,
or a transformed parameter. If not, the values might be able to be
recomputed.

Loops involving only arithmetic on double values, like the above,
are very fast in Stan.

- Bob

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] assigning random effects to observations
parts:
On 4/5/13 12:51 AM, Kyle Foreman wrote:
> Sorry, should have reattached the model to the latest email! It's attached here. In this version I've put the desired
> quantity (log_mu) plus the interim ones not needed (beta1_stz & beta1_long) in transformed parameters. I'll stick with
> this for now, will see if it's still tenable in terms of memory when I get to the full implementation.

Given that the variables you don't
need to store show up only in the transformed parameters
block, this is easy. You just want to replace your:

transformed parameters {
vector[N] log_mu; // need to store this
vector[S] beta1_stz; // don't need to store this
vector[N] beta1_long; // don't need to store this

beta1_stz <- beta1 - mean(beta1);
for (n in 1:N)
beta1_long[n] <- beta1_stz[state[n]];

log_mu <- log_pop + alpha0 + (alpha1 * year) + beta1_long;
}

with this:

transformed parameters {
vector[N] log_mu; // need to store this
{
vector[S] beta1_stz; // don't need to store this
vector[N] beta1_long; // don't need to store this

beta1_stz <- beta1 - mean(beta1);
for (n in 1:N)
beta1_long[n] <- beta1_stz[state[n]];

log_mu <- log_pop + alpha0 + (alpha1 * year) + beta1_long;
}
}

That makes beta1_stz and beta1_long local variables, but exposes
log_mu to the model.

> And what I meant by "prevents vectorization" was that I had to use a loop like
> |
> for (n in 1:N)
> log_mu[n] <- log_pop[n] + alpha0 + (alpha1 * year[n]) + (beta1[state[n]] - mean(beta1));
> |
> instead of vector addition/multiplication like
> |
> log_mu <- log_pop + alpha0 + (alpha1 * year) +beta1_long;

Looping, assignment and arithmetic are all compiled to C++,
so they're much faster than in an interpreted language.
In fact, the loop version can be faster because it doesn't
do any intermediate allocations of vectors.

Where you get a big boost from vectorization in Stan
is where there's a reduction, such as a dot product, that takes
two vectors and produces a scalar. For those, we can partially
evaluate the derivatives so the gradients are computed much faster.
Same for the sampling statements with vectorized inputs.

- Bob

parts: Thanks Bob, that's great! I guess I didn't understand "Stan allows local variables to be declared in blocks" (from the manual) - I was thinking about that in terms of loops, didn't think to extrapolate...
On Fri, Apr 5, 2013 at 10:45 PM, Bob Carpenter <ca...@alias-i.com> wrote:

On 4/5/13 12:51 AM, Kyle Foreman wrote:
Sorry, should have reattached the model to the latest email! It's attached here. In this version I've put the desired
quantity (log_mu) plus the interim ones not needed (beta1_stz & beta1_long) in transformed parameters. I'll stick with
this for now, will see if it's still tenable in terms of memory when I get to the full implementation.

Given that the variables you don't
need to store show up only in the transformed parameters
block, this is easy.  You just want to replace your:

  transformed parameters {
    vector[N] log_mu;       // need to store this
    vector[S] beta1_stz;    // don't need to store this
    vector[N] beta1_long;   // don't need to store this

    beta1_stz <- beta1 - mean(beta1);
    for (n in 1:N)
        beta1_long[n] <- beta1_stz[state[n]];
    log_mu <- log_pop + alpha0 + (alpha1 * year) + beta1_long;
  }

with this:

  transformed parameters {
    vector[N] log_mu;       // need to store this
    {
       vector[S] beta1_stz;    // don't need to store this
       vector[N] beta1_long;   // don't need to store this

       beta1_stz <- beta1 - mean(beta1);
       for (n in 1:N)
          beta1_long[n] <- beta1_stz[state[n]];
       log_mu <- log_pop + alpha0 + (alpha1 * year) + beta1_long;
    }
}

That makes beta1_stz and beta1_long local variables, but exposes
log_mu to the model.


And what I meant by "prevents vectorization" was that I had to use a loop like
|
for (n in 1:N)
     log_mu[n] <- log_pop[n] + alpha0 + (alpha1 * year[n]) + (beta1[state[n]] - mean(beta1));
|
instead of vector addition/multiplication like
|
log_mu <- log_pop + alpha0 + (alpha1 * year) +beta1_long;

Looping, assignment and arithmetic are all compiled to C++,
so they're much faster than in an interpreted language.
In fact, the loop version can be faster because it doesn't
do any intermediate allocations of vectors.

Where you get a big boost from vectorization in Stan
is where there's a reduction, such as a dot product, that takes
two vectors and produces a scalar.  For those, we can partially
evaluate the derivatives so the gradients are computed much faster.
Same for the sampling statements with vectorized inputs.
- Bob
